html:
The first Moon landing was the Apollo 11 mission of the US space agency NASA, which put two astronauts on the Moon on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface, while Michael Collins circled overhead.

It was the climax of the space race between the United States and the Soviet Union. The Soviets had launched the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957 and the first man in space, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961. Stung, President John F. Kennedy set the goal in 1961 of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out. The Apollo program that followed employed around 400,000 people at its peak.

The mission launched on 16 July on a Saturn V rocket from Florida. Four days later the lunar module Eagle landed on the Sea of Tranquillity, with fuel running low after Armstrong steered past a field of boulders. Stepping onto the surface, he said: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." The two men spent about two and a half hours outside, collected rock samples, set up experiments and planted a US flag. Hundreds of millions of people watched on television. All three returned safely on 24 July.

Five more Apollo missions landed, the last in 1972, and twelve men in all have walked on the Moon. The race pushed forward rockets, computers and miniature electronics. Photos of Earth seen from space also helped inspire the environmental movement. It came just 66 years after the Wright Flyer.
